lesson.title: Build an ls-style CLI in Rust with Clap, Tabled and Serde
lesson.goal: build a command-line tool in Rust with cargo that parses arguments

sources.title: Build an ls-style CLI in Rust with Clap, Tabled and Serde

steps.title: Create project and parse path
steps.instructions: Run `cargo new best_ls`, add clap with the derive feature to Cargo.toml, and define a `#[derive(Parser)]` struct with an `Option<PathBuf>` field, then call `Cli::parse()` in main. Verify with `cargo run -- -h` that usage/help is printed.

targets.caption: Add clap with the derive feature
Define the Cli struct with an optional path
Parse command-line arguments in main
clap generates the help text automatically

explanations.topic: clap's derive feature makes argument parsing easy
Taking a path as the first positional argument
The Parser trait adds the parse method
Using -- to pass arguments through cargo run
Auto-generated usage, arguments and options sections

hints: Add clap to Cargo.toml under [dependencies] and enable the "derive" feature.
Put #[derive(Parser)] on your struct and import it with `use clap::Parser;`.
Give the struct one field, `path: Option<PathBuf>`, and import `std::path::PathBuf`.
In main, call `let cli = Cli::parse();`, then run `cargo run -- -h` to see the help.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `features = ["derive"]` on clap, so #[derive(Parser)] doesn't exist.
Not importing the Parser trait, which causes 'no function or associated item named parse'.
Running `cargo run -h` without `--`, which shows cargo's help instead of your app's.
Missing `use std::path::PathBuf;`.
Using `PathBuf` instead of `Option<PathBuf>`, which makes the path required (it shows <PATH> instead of [PATH]).

steps.title: Add version, about, default path
steps.instructions: Add `#[command(version, about, long_about = ...)]` to the struct and check `cargo run -- --version`. In main default the path with `unwrap_or(PathBuf::from("."))` and print `path.display()`.

targets.caption: Add version, about and long_about
Default the path to "."
Run with and without a path argument

explanations.topic: #[command(version)] auto-generates a --version flag
long_about text shown in --help
path is an Option, so unwrap_or supplies a default
Defaulting to the current directory like ls

hints: Clap reads struct-level settings from a #[command(...)] attribute placed above the struct.
Try #[command(version, about, long_about = "...")], then run `cargo run -- --version`.
cli.path is an Option<PathBuf>; use .unwrap_or(PathBuf::from(".")) to get a default.
PathBuf doesn't implement Display, so print it with println!("{}", path.display()).
common_mistakes: Forgetting the `--` in `cargo run -- --version`, so cargo prints its own version instead of your app's.
Writing #[clap(...)] or misspelling long_about (e.g. longabout).
Printing the PathBuf directly with {} and getting a 'doesn't implement Display' error.
Not importing std::path::PathBuf.

steps.title: Check path existence with colors
steps.instructions: In src/main.rs use `if let Ok(does_exist) = fs::exists(&path)` and print "Path does not exist" with owo-colors `.red()` when false, or "Error reading directory" on Err. Add owo-colors to Cargo.toml and run `cargo run -- longpath` to see the red message.

targets.caption: Check whether the path exists
Add the owo-colors crate
Red message for a bad path

explanations.topic: fs::exists reports whether a path exists
owo-colors crate for colored terminal output
cargo build puts the binary in target/debug
fs::exists returns Err when existence can't be determined

hints: Wrap the check in `if let Ok(does_exist) = fs::exists(&path)` and branch on `does_exist`.
Add `owo-colors` to [dependencies] in Cargo.toml, or run `cargo add owo-colors`.
Bring the trait into scope with `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;` so `"text".red()` works.
Pass the bad path after `--`: `cargo run -- longpath`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;`, which gives a 'no method named red' error.
Writing the crate name as `owo_colors` in Cargo.toml. The package name is `owo-colors`.
Leaving out the `--` in `cargo run -- longpath`, so the argument goes to cargo and not to your program.
Using `fs::exists(path)` without `&`, which moves `path` before later use.
Not handling the Err branch with an 'Error reading directory' message.

steps.title: List directory file names
steps.instructions: In src/main.rs write `fn get_files(path: &Path) -> Vec<String>` that iterates `fs::read_dir(path)` and pushes each entry's file name (falling back to "unknown name"). Loop over `get_files(&path)` in main, print each name, and run `cargo run`.

targets.caption: New helper that returns the directory's file names
Fall back to "unknown name" when the name isn't valid UTF-8
cargo run lists the current directory

explanations.topic: Creating a helper fn that takes a path and returns Vec<String>
if let Ok(...) on fs::read_dir to handle read errors
Iterating entries and converting file_name() with into_string().unwrap_or
Passing &path to get_files and printing each name

hints: Write a function that takes `&Path` and returns `Vec<String>`. Create an empty vector at the start and return it at the end.
Use `if let Ok(read_dir) = fs::read_dir(path)`, then `for entry in read_dir`, and `if let Ok(file) = entry` for each entry.
`file.file_name()` returns an OsString. Call `.into_string().unwrap_or("unknown name".into())` to get a String, then push it.
In main, loop with `for file in get_files(&path) { println!("{}", file); }` and run `cargo run`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use std::fs;` or `use std::path::Path;`.
Passing `path` instead of `&path` to get_files, which moves the PathBuf or mismatches the type.
Using `.unwrap()` on read_dir or entry, which panics on unreadable directories instead of skipping them.
Trying to push `file.file_name()` directly, which is an OsString, not a String.
Declaring the vector without `mut`, so `push` fails to compile.

steps.title: Collect metadata into FileEntry
steps.instructions: Define `struct FileEntry` and `enum EntryType { File, Dir }` (deriving Debug and strum's Display) and fill entries from `fs::metadata(&file.path())` in a `map_data` function. Make get_files return `Vec<FileEntry>`, debug-print it with `{:#?}`, and run `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Struct holding each file's metadata
File or Dir, with strum's Display derive
Turns a dir entry into a FileEntry
Pretty-printed metadata from cargo run

explanations.topic: Designing a FileEntry struct for file metadata
`type` is a reserved word, so the field is named e_type
Using strum's Display derive to print enums as strings
if let Ok on fs::metadata, which returns a Result
Bug: passing the dir path instead of file.path() to metadata
Extracting the logic into a map_data function

hints: Make a struct with a name String, an e_type field of a new EntryType enum, a u64 byte length and a modified String. Have get_files return a Vec of it.
fs::metadata returns a Result, so use `if let Ok(meta) = fs::metadata(&file.path())`. Then pick EntryType::Dir or EntryType::File with `meta.is_dir()`, and get the size with `meta.len()`.
Add strum (with the derive feature) to Cargo.toml, then write `#[derive(Debug, Display)]` on the enum. Put `#[derive(Debug)]` on the struct and print with `println!("{:#?}", entries)`.
If every entry shows the same size or type, you are reading the metadata of the directory itself. Pass `&file.path()`, not the directory path.
common_mistakes: Naming the field `type`. That is a Rust keyword, so use e_type or r#type.
Calling fs::metadata on the directory path instead of file.path(). Every entry then shows identical metadata.
Using `if let Some(...)` on fs::metadata. It returns a Result, so use Ok.
Forgetting `#[derive(Debug)]` on FileEntry or EntryType, so `{:#?}` fails to compile.
Adding strum without the derive feature (or strum_macros), so `use strum::Display` doesn't resolve.
Not changing get_files' return type to Vec<FileEntry>, or forgetting to return the vector.

steps.title: Render a colored table
steps.instructions: Add tabled, derive `Tabled` on FileEntry and EntryType's struct field, build `Table::new(get_files(&path))`, apply `Style::rounded()` and `table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN)` plus colors for other columns and `Rows::first()` bright green. Rename headers with `#[tabled(rename = "Type")]`, `"Name"`, `"Size B"` and print the table.

targets.caption: Build the table from get_files
Rename column headers
Rounded colored table output

explanations.topic: What the tabled crate does: print structs as ASCII tables
Applying a table style (rounded)
Targeting columns/rows with modify to add colors
Renaming headers with #[tabled(rename)]

hints: Add tabled to Cargo.toml (cargo add tabled) and derive Tabled on FileEntry.
Every field type in a Tabled struct must implement Display, so EntryType needs a Display impl or derive.
Create the table with Table::new(get_files(&path)), call table.with(Style::rounded()), then println!("{}", table).
Color columns with table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN), and the header with Rows::first().
common_mistakes: Forgetting to derive Tabled on FileEntry, so Table::new fails to compile.
EntryType not implementing Display, which tabled requires for every field.
Wrong import paths: Style, Color, Columns and Rows live under tabled::settings.
Not declaring table as mut before calling with/modify.
Using Columns::single/one with an out-of-range index, so the color does nothing.

steps.title: Format modified date with chrono
steps.instructions: Add chrono to Cargo.toml and in map_data use `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified()` to convert to `DateTime<Utc>` and format it with `%a %b %e %Y`, else an empty string. Run `cargo run -- src` to see the dates in the table.

targets.caption: Convert SystemTime into DateTime<Utc> with if let Ok
Format string for the Modified column
Build done; table shows dates

explanations.topic: chrono crate for dates and times
metadata.modified() returns Result<SystemTime>
Converting SystemTime to DateTime<Utc> via into()
strftime-style format specifiers

hints: Add chrono to Cargo.toml under [dependencies] (or run `cargo add chrono`).
meta.modified() returns a Result. Use `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified() { ... } else { String::new() }`.
Annotate the conversion so `into()` knows its target: `let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into();`, then `date.format("%a %b %e %Y").to_string()`.
Import with `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};` and run `cargo run -- src`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add chrono to Cargo.toml, which causes an 'unresolved import chrono' error.
Leaving out the DateTime<Utc> type annotation, so `.into()` can't infer its target type.
Naming the binding `mod`, which is a reserved keyword. Use something like `modi`.
Not returning a String in the else branch, so the if/else arms have mismatched types.
Running `cargo run src` without `--`, or with a path that doesn't exist.

steps.title: Add --json output flag
steps.instructions: Add `#[arg(short, long)] json: bool` to Cli, extract the table code into `print_table`, and when `cli.json` is set print `serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string())`. Add serde (derive) and serde_json, derive `Serialize` on FileEntry and EntryType, and test with `cargo run -- -j` and `--json`.

targets.caption: New --json / -j flag on the Cli struct
Table rendering extracted into its own function
Serialize the file list to JSON
JSON file list output

explanations.topic: #[arg(short, long)] creates both -j and --json flags
Using serde + serde_json to serialize structs to JSON
Every nested type (EntryType enum) must also derive Serialize
unwrap_or provides a fallback string if serialization fails

hints: Add a `json: bool` field to your Cli struct with `#[arg(short, long)]` so clap generates -j and --json.
Run `cargo add serde --features derive` and `cargo add serde_json`, then `use serde::Serialize;`.
Derive Serialize on both FileEntry and the EntryType enum; the struct won't compile otherwise.
In main: `if cli.json { println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string())); } else { print_table(path); }`
common_mistakes: Adding `json: bool` without `#[arg(short, long)]`, so it becomes a required positional argument instead of a flag.
Forgetting the `derive` feature on serde, so `#[derive(Serialize)]` is not found.
Deriving Serialize on FileEntry but not on EntryType, which causes a trait-bound compile error.
Running `cargo run -j` instead of `cargo run -- -j`, which passes the flag to cargo rather than the program.
Passing `get_files(path)` by value after `path` was moved into print_table, causing a use-after-move error.
